paragraphs.text: [[**abducens nucleus:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A brainstem group containing the motor neurons recorded in the eye-drift study. Their axons activate the lateral rectus eye muscle.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for abducens nucleus.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Connects the recorded brainstem group to the eye muscle.

paragraphs.text: [[**activity bump:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A localized peak of population firing rates across neurons ordered by their preferred represented values.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for activity bump.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Distinguishes a population peak across preferred values from a trajectory in space.

paragraphs.text: [[**attractor manifold:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The continuous family of persistent activity states, described by its represented coordinates rather than by every neural activity separately.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for attractor manifold.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Separates represented coordinates from the full neural state.

paragraphs.text: [[**Betti numbers:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Counts of independent connected components, loops, cavities, and their higher-dimensional counterparts.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Betti numbers.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Names the separate component, loop and cavity counts.

paragraphs.text: [[**Brownian motion:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous random process starting at zero with independent Gaussian increments of mean zero and variance equal to elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Brownian motion.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Keeps increment independence and the unit variance-time convention together.

paragraphs.text: [[**causal filter:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A rule whose current output depends only on present and past input.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for causal filter.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Excludes future inputs from the present output.

paragraphs.text: [[**coefficient of determination:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} For the optimal linear prediction with an intercept, the fraction of response variance removed by prediction. With one predictor it equals the squared correlation.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for coefficient of determination.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Retains the fitted-intercept and optimal-linear-prediction conditions.

paragraphs.text: [[**coefficient of variation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Standard deviation divided by mean. In the spike-train discussion it is applied to interspike intervals.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for coefficient of variation.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Identifies both the ratio and its interval application.

paragraphs.text: [[**continuous attractor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and neutral motion along it in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for continuous attractor.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Distinguishes restoring transverse dynamics from neutral motion along the family.

paragraphs.text: [[**convolution:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An integral or sum combining past input values with a shifted response kernel to obtain a filtered output.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = NO -->

review.purpose: Provide lookup for convolution.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Connects the response kernel to accumulated past-input effects.

paragraphs.text: [[**correlation coefficient:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Covariance divided by the product of standard deviations, giving a dimensionless measure of linear association.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = YES -->

review.purpose: Provide lookup for correlation coefficient.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Keeps normalization distinct from raw covariance.

paragraphs.text: [[**covariance:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The mean product of two centered random variables, measuring their shared variation.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for covariance.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Specifies centered products rather than raw coactivation.

paragraphs.text: [[**Cramér Rao bound:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A lower bound on local unbiased estimation variance under the required regularity conditions, expressed through inverse Fisher information.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Cramér Rao bound.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Limits the variance claim to local unbiased estimation and regularity.

paragraphs.text: [[**critical point:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point where a function's gradient is zero. The Euler calculation also requires invertible Hessians.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for critical point.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Separates zero gradient from the additional invertible-Hessian assumption.

paragraphs.text: [[**decoding:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Estimating a represented value from neural responses.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for decoding.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Identifies the direction from responses to represented value.

paragraphs.text: [[**dendrite:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A branching input structure of a neuron.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for dendrite.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Identifies the cell structure that receives input.

paragraphs.text: [[**diffusion coefficient:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The coefficient $D$ in the local one-dimensional displacement variance $2Dt$. Its units are coordinate squared per time.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for diffusion coefficient.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Preserves the factor two and coordinate-squared/time units.

paragraphs.text: [[**diffusion tensor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The matrix giving local coordinate-displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for diffusion tensor.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Extends the variance convention to cross-coordinate covariances.

paragraphs.text: [[**Dirac delta:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} A point-mass distribution. In the initial-condition equation all probability is concentrated at the specified coordinate.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Dirac delta.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Connects the formal object to concentrated initial probability.

paragraphs.text: [[**displacement:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The change in a coordinate between two observations. For eye angle, $\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)$ over lag $\ell$.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for displacement.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Specifies a difference across a lag rather than an absolute coordinate.

paragraphs.text: [[**encoding:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Establishing a population activity pattern from an input.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for encoding.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Identifies the input-to-population-pattern direction.

paragraphs.text: [[**Euler characteristic:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The alternating sum of Betti numbers. In three dimensions, components minus independent loops plus enclosed cavities.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Euler characteristic.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Keeps the alternating signs of topological counts.

paragraphs.text: [[**excess kurtosis:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The fourth centered moment divided by the squared variance, minus three. It is zero for a Gaussian population.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for excess kurtosis.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Distinguishes the centered fourth-moment statistic from ordinary kurtosis.

paragraphs.text: [[**excitatory input:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} In the models used here, an input that increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for excitatory input.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Names an effect on firing tendency within the model.

paragraphs.text: [[**excursion set:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} The positions where a function exceeds a specified level.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for excursion set.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Identifies the domain points selected by a level.

paragraphs.text: [[**Fano factor:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} Spike-count variance divided by mean count, for a specified counting interval and condition.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Fano factor.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Retains the counting interval and condition.

review.reason: Separates expectation from an individual spike realization.

review.purpose: Provide lookup for Fisher information.
review.connection: An independent glossary entry in alphabetical lookup order; its teaching dependency is the relevant main chapter, not the previous glossary item.
review.reason: Connects the score to local parameter sensitivity.

review.reason: Separates slow fixation motion from rapid eye movements.

review.reason: Refers to zero deterministic change, not absent noise.

paragraphs.text: [[**Fokker Planck equation:**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} An equation describing how a probability density evolves under drift and diffusion. The guide states the convention before using it.]{.definition-explanation}

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. [Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system.]{.key-statement} The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

review.purpose: Connect eye holding, location tracking and the three paper questions.
review.connection: Introduces the common persistence problem before cellular terms.
review.reason: Needed to show why the different papers belong together.

paragraphs.text: Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know how its activity represents that value and what makes the activity variable. We begin with the spikes that cells send and the patterns of firing rates across a population. A model of spike counts then shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. We then learn how to tell whether measurements vary together and how to separate random spreading from a change in the average value. Those distinctions will let us interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion.

review.purpose: Set the prerequisite order from spikes to variability and shared changes.
review.connection: Bridges the common problem to the first neural definitions.
review.reason: The sequence explains why signal meaning precedes memory dynamics.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> [A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called [**spike**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} [A [**firing rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the expected number of spikes per unit time.]{.definition-explanation} A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES -->

review.purpose: Define spikes and expected firing rate.
review.connection: Starts the cellular account before synaptic effects.
review.reason: The 20 Hz example prevents treating rate as a clock.

paragraphs.text: [Neurons affect one another through connections called [**synapse**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects:

review.purpose: Define synapses as connections between neurons.
review.connection: Turns individual spike events into interactions.
review.reason: Needed before excitatory and inhibitory effects can have a receiving cell.

paragraphs.text: [An [**excitatory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Define excitation by increased firing tendency.
review.connection: Supplies one outcome of the preceding synapse model.
review.reason: The later sign of a positive weight depends on this meaning.

paragraphs.text: [An [**inhibitory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} reduces it.]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Define inhibition by reduced firing tendency.
review.connection: Completes the paired effects before recurrent feedback.
review.reason: Needed to interpret mutually inhibiting cells later.

paragraphs.text: The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. [When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has [**recurrent connectivity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears.

review.purpose: Explain persistence of synaptic effects and recurrent feedback.
review.connection: Connects brief spikes to activity after an external signal ends.
review.reason: Supplies the biological reason a memory model can have lasting activity.

paragraphs.text: [A [**tuning curve**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} gives a neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation} For eye angle $\theta$, a simple local model is $r_i(\theta)=b_i+k_i\theta$. Neuron $i$ has baseline rate $b_i$ in spikes per second and slope $k_i$ in spikes per second per degree. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.[^f-eye]

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> For changing rates, the expected count is the integral $\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt$. In a recurrent network, $r(t)$ itself depends on past activity. The useful independence statement is therefore conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. Averaging over the changing state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

paragraphs.text: During fixation, a monkey tries to keep looking at a stationary target, yet its eye moves slightly. A changing command from the brain can make many motor neurons change their firing together. Their spikes act on the eye muscles, which turn the eye. An individual motor neuron also adds spike variability of its own. The 2022 paper asks how much of the observed movement follows a shared neural command, and whether that command itself wanders over time.[^f-eye]

review.purpose: Describe shared commands, private neuron noise and eye movement.
review.connection: Turns spike variability into a concrete physiological question.
review.reason: Supplies the pathway and measured outcome before introducing covariance.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedSubject = NO --> [Covariance asks which recorded changes occur together. Displacement statistics ask how far the eye moves and how that movement grows with elapsed time.]{.key-statement} Neither measurement by itself identifies the neural circuit responsible. <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedSubject = YES -->

review.purpose: Separate the questions answered by covariance and displacement statistics.
review.connection: Organizes the two tools before their explanations.
review.reason: The circuit-identification limit prevents mistaking a statistic for a unique mechanism.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> **Physical meaning: a shared command can survive averaging across neurons.** If a common input raises the firing of many motor neurons that pull the eye in the same direction, their effects add. Independent extra and missing spikes partly cancel when those neurons act together. The paper compares the measured eye displacement with a displacement predicted from one neuron's spikes, after converting both to degrees. That prediction is an analysis of a recording, not an extra command sent to the muscles. A relationship between the two is evidence to test against a model of shared input and private noise. It does not mean that the one recorded cell causes all the movement. <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

review.purpose: Explain why common commands survive population averaging.
review.connection: Connects the pathway to predicted and measured displacements.
review.reason: Clarifies that the prediction is an analysis, not an extra muscle command.

paragraphs.text: [**Covariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [measures whether two signals tend to be above their own averages together or on opposite sides of those averages.]{.definition-explanation} Positive covariance between the two displacements means that above-average changes in the neural prediction tend to accompany above-average changes in eye position. [The [**correlation coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\rho$, expresses this shared variation relative to the spread of each signal.]{.definition-explanation} Extra private noise can lower $\rho$ even when the shared drive has not weakened. The [eye-drift calculation](ch-eye-drift.html#sec-eye-chi) explains why a modest correlation need not mean a small shared contribution to movement.

review.purpose: Define covariance and normalized correlation physically.
review.connection: Precedes formal definitions with the meaning of shared variation.
review.reason: The private-noise example explains why modest correlation can coexist with common drive.

paragraphs.text: **Physical meaning: random wandering differs from a persistent directional error.** Let $x(t)$ be horizontal eye angle in degrees and let $\ell$ be the time between two measurements, called the lag, in seconds. [The [**displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)$ is the change in that angle.]{.definition-explanation} A random change in the maintained command can move the eye left in one interval and right in another. The average displacement can then be close to zero while individual displacements are large. A persistent imbalance in the command can instead make the average displacement grow in one direction. Muscles smooth the command before it becomes eye movement, so the timescale of the observation also matters.

review.purpose: Explain lag, displacement and random versus directional movement.
review.connection: Starts the second physical question after shared variation.
review.reason: Provides observable meanings before the MSD identity.

paragraphs.text: **Random changes in the stored command:** more frequent or larger lasting changes make the stored angle spread faster. paragraphs.text: **A persistent directional imbalance:** this changes the mean displacement. In a constant-velocity approximation, doubling that velocity doubles the mean displacement at a fixed lag and quadruples its squared contribution to MSD. <!-- vale ai-tells.LabelAndExplain = YES -->

paragraphs.text: The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory]

review.purpose: Distinguish activity changes from changes in the represented value.
review.connection: Connects population coding to the geometry of memory error.
review.reason: Explains why stable-looking firing can still be inaccurate.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> We first build a small example in which some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES -->

review.purpose: Order restoring disturbances, accumulated error and fixed spatial randomness.
review.connection: Prepares the chapter's progression.
review.reason: Each step answers a different consequence of variable neural signals.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeKeeps = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> Imagine a group of neurons maintaining a pattern that represents an eye angle after a movement command has ended. Random spikes disturb that pattern. Recurrent input can correct some disturbances by changing the cells' firing back toward a persistent pattern. But if a disturbance produces the pattern for a different angle, an ideal memory circuit has no record of which angle was originally intended. [Keeping a pattern stable is therefore different from keeping the stored value correct.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeKeeps = YES -->

review.purpose: Explain why a different stable pattern cannot identify the original angle.
review.connection: Gives the physical problem before state-space terms.
review.reason: Makes neutral memory directions meaningful before equations.

paragraphs.text: [A circuit's current activities are its [**state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. [A [**fixed point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation} It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays.

review.purpose: Define state, fixed point and directional stability.
review.connection: Supplies the dynamical vocabulary for continuous attractors.
review.reason: The definitions specify what changes and what decays.

paragraphs.text: Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. [A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation} [The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit.]{.definition-explanation} A line attractor has one represented coordinate. A ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.[^f-memory]

review.purpose: Define the continuous family, neutral direction and manifold dimension.
review.connection: Extends one fixed point to a representation of continuous values.
review.reason: Separates represented dimensions from neuron count.

paragraphs.text: In the illustrative two-cell model below, the difference between the firing rates represents the angle. Raising both rates equally leaves that difference unchanged. The model's feedback removes the common increase. Raising one rate while lowering the other changes the represented angle. That second change persists. The calculation makes these two responses explicit. It is not a fitted biological circuit.

paragraphs.text: To calculate the loss of accuracy, we first describe how spikes renew synaptic activity as it decays. We then follow a small disturbance through the circuit's return toward a stable pattern and identify the change in stored value that remains. Adding these lasting random changes gives a local rate of spreading. When connections have equal weights in both directions, we can express that rate using the cells' tuning curves and check its meaning in a two-cell example. The following chapter extends this local prediction to longer delays.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> A spike from cell $j$ raises $s_j$ by one and therefore changes the input to cell $i$ by $W_{ij}$. That contribution then decays over time $\tau$. For an increasing transfer function, a positive weight raises the receiving cell's rate and a negative weight lowers it. The resulting new spikes affect other cells in turn. Thus the weights set where a disturbance goes, the transfer function sets the rate response, and $\tau$ sets how long each synaptic contribution lasts. The input $g_i$ is in the model's input units. It is not specified as a measured membrane voltage. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

Increasing population size therefore keeps the mean dynamics fixed and reduces input fluctuations. paragraphs.text: We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows.

paragraphs.text: Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift.

review.purpose: Recall current/initial coordinates and the origin of local D.
review.connection: Reconnects notation to the prior projection calculation.
review.reason: States the constant-D conditions before using 2Dt again.

paragraphs.text: **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded.

review.purpose: Hold D fixed to isolate the effect of coordinate boundaries.
review.connection: Starts the line-circle comparison with a controlled mechanism.
review.reason: The later plateau cannot be mistaken for a changed noise strength.

paragraphs.text: **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$. Constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions.

review.purpose: Define trial density and the Itô evaluation convention.
review.connection: Prepares the density equation before state-dependent noise use.
review.reason: The unfamiliar stochastic convention has an operational meaning.

paragraphs.text: To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives

review.purpose: Taylor-expand a smooth test function using conditional increment moments.
review.connection: Starts the optional derivation from random steps to density.
review.reason: Uses the stated mean and variance rather than an unexplained PDE rule.

paragraphs.text: The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives

review.purpose: Average over initial states and pass to the time derivative.
review.connection: Connects the local expansion to a density integral.
review.reason: Explains the limiting step and higher-order remainder.

paragraphs.text: Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below.

review.purpose: State boundary conditions and integrate by parts twice.
review.connection: Completes the optional derivation of the density equation.
review.reason: The derivatives act on Dp for a stated reason.

paragraphs.text: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation}

review.purpose: Name and display the zero-drift Fokker Planck equation.
review.connection: Places the result outside its derivation fold.
review.reason: The main path has the evolution law needed for line and circle comparisons.

paragraphs.text: [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is

review.purpose: Explain the point-mass initial condition and Gaussian line solution.
review.connection: Interprets the PDE symbols before using its solution.
review.reason: Distinguishes Dirac delta from the earlier Kronecker symbol.

paragraphs.text: Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is

review.purpose: Wrap the line density and compute the uniform-circle limit.
review.connection: Connects the same local diffusion to a bounded angular error.
review.reason: Provides the actual limiting integral and reporting convention.

paragraphs.text: **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$.

review.purpose: Introduce mutual excitation as a state-dependent-noise example.
review.connection: Moves from fixed-D boundaries to changing local rates.
review.reason: The weights, biases and fixed states are supplied before projection.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeFires = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> Here $\theta$ is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when $\theta>|b_0|/2$. When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other's firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger $\theta$ raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeFires = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

review.purpose: Explain the persistent common change and restoring difference.
review.connection: Gives the excitation example's physical mechanism.
review.reason: The activation coordinate and positive-rate domain avoid inheriting an angle interpretation.

paragraphs.text: **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives

review.purpose: State the Itô state-dependent process and its moment equations.
review.connection: Connects the neural example to the density machinery.
review.reason: The zero-drift and boundary conditions remain visible.

The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = YES -->

review.purpose: Derive moment identities and the short-time expansion.
review.connection: Follows the stated PDE with explicit integration operations.

paragraphs.text: **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]

paragraphs.text: **Neural mechanism.** [Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate systematic drift, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = YES -->

review.connection: Connects the no-drift assumption to what microscopic analysis would be needed.
review.reason: Avoids presenting tuning of the noise-free model as a complete noisy-drift proof.

paragraphs.text: **Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network.

review.purpose: Define Stratonovich evaluation and show the conversion drift.
review.connection: Uses the earlier Itô definition to distinguish two written noise equations.
review.reason: Explains the origin and limited role of the D-prime-over-two estimate.

paragraphs.text: With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$.

review.purpose: Compare the orders of random and mean displacement.
review.connection: Connects the drift estimate to the large-population approximation.
review.reason: Shows why leading variance and smaller mean effects can require different care.

paragraphs.text: **Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift. They cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average.]{.key-statement} A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions.

review.purpose: Distinguish cancelling mean drift from cancelling individual noise increments.
review.connection: Interprets the preceding orders and possible tuning.
review.reason: Preserves the remaining diffusion even with known drift compensation.

paragraphs.text: The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. A matching calculation of information would need the probabilities of joint spike patterns. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)). It does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation]

review.purpose: State conditional spike independence and the correlated-noise extension.
review.connection: Closes scope before interpreting the figures.
review.reason: The covariance matrix and joint-pattern likelihood explain what would change.

paragraphs.text: **Neural mechanism in the figures.** [Figure 1A, p. 2](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-1) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization).

review.connection: Connects the earlier left projection to the original figure.

paragraphs.text: A neuron that receives spikes from a memory circuit can use them to estimate the value stored by that circuit. [Collecting more spikes helps distinguish nearby activity patterns, but during collection the pattern itself keeps moving.]{.key-statement} The same variability that limits readout also perturbs the recurrent network. Burak and Fiete connect these two effects by deriving a lower bound on memory diffusion from the information in the spikes.[^p1-info-main]

review.purpose: Connect finite-spike estimation and the same noise inside the recurrent circuit.
review.connection: Opens information from the preceding dynamics and figure distinction.
review.reason: Explains why readout accuracy can constrain memory motion.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> The useful quantity is how clearly a short spike sample distinguishes nearby memory values. Comparing that quantity with the random motion already derived gives a minimum rate of memory spreading. This is a limit for a particular network, so using it to compare different networks also requires keeping track of what changes and what stays fixed. More information can permit better stability without ensuring that a particular circuit achieves it. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->

review.purpose: Introduce local distinguishability and distinguish a bound from achieved stability.
review.connection: Prepares a measure of information before formal definitions.
review.reason: Prevents a lower bound from becoming a claim about actual improvement.

paragraphs.text: We retain the memory coordinate $\theta$, initial value $\Theta$, firing rate $\bar r_i(\theta)$, synaptic time constant $\tau$, and diffusion convention $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D\Delta t$. The [network projection](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value.

review.purpose: Recall shared coordinates, rates, time constant and diffusion convention.
review.connection: Links the statistical calculation to the existing projection model.
review.reason: The two quantities will refer to the same network and coordinate.

paragraphs.text: **Neural mechanism.** Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction.

review.purpose: Explain distinguishability through rate change relative to variability.
review.connection: Gives the physical meaning before the likelihood formula.
review.reason: The reader can interpret information without knowing its formal name.

paragraphs.text: In a short interval $h$, let $n_i$ be neuron $i$'s count. Treat the memory state as locally constant and use the conditionally independent Poisson approximation from the neural model. The calculation below uses positive rates.

review.purpose: Specify short-bin counts, positive rates and locally fixed state.
review.connection: Applies the established conditional Poisson model.
review.reason: Places the information calculation's conditions before its product likelihood.

review.connection: Turns observed spikes into a function of candidate memory value.
review.reason: Introduces the unfamiliar statistical tool before differentiation.

[[**Fisher information**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is this expected squared score. paragraphs.text: **Interpretation.** [This is the [**Cramér Rao bound**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It is a local bound for regular unbiased estimation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not guarantee that every finite spike sample admits an estimator attaining it. The paper works in a weak noise, informative sample regime where local likelihoods can be approximated as Gaussian and a suitable estimator can approach the bound. [A [**prior distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the spikes.]{.definition-explanation} A strong prior, bias, boundaries, or globally ambiguous tuning changes the estimation problem.[^p1-cr]

review.purpose: Name the Cramér Rao bound and explain its local limits and priors.
review.connection: Interprets the proof before treating the result as an observation model.
review.reason: Attainability, bias and prior knowledge are not assumed away silently.

paragraphs.text: If the coordinate is an angle in radians, $J$ has units $\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The information in a locally stationary interval of duration $h$ is $Jh$, not $J$.[^p1-fi-source] A vanishing rate requires a suitable limit and regularity of the likelihood.

review.connection: Clarifies the scale used by later readout equations.
review.reason: Prevents mistaking an information rate for the information in a sample.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> Each cell contributes squared slope divided by its count variance per unit time. High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell's peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network's present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates. <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->

review.connection: Connects the formula to neural tuning before the figure example.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.HedgingPhrases = NO --> **Neural mechanism.** [The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed.]{.key-statement} Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input. <!-- vale ai-tells.HedgingPhrases = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES -->

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> **Mathematical derivation.** Increasing $N$ while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as $1/N$ keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as $N$ in the numerator and $N^2$ in the denominator. Consequently $D\propto1/N$, while $J\propto N$. This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

review.purpose: Derive population-number scaling under replication and weight adjustment.
review.connection: Gives the first controlled comparison.
review.reason: Adding arbitrary neurons is explicitly a different operation.

paragraphs.text: If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor $a$, their slopes are also multiplied by $a$, so $J\mapsto aJ$. For equality achieving exponential networks, $D\mapsto D/a$ immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves $g_i'$ up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper's rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.[^p1-scaling]

review.purpose: Derive rate scaling and state when tuning geometry is preserved.
review.connection: Adds firing-rate comparison after neuron count.
review.reason: Prevents changing one numerator while overlooking slopes or the attractor.

paragraphs.text: Changing $\tau$ while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives $D\propto\tau^{-2}$ in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because $\bar s=\tau\bar r$.

review.purpose: State the fixed-rate-tuning synaptic-time comparison.
review.connection: Introduces the inverse-square result with its control conditions.
review.reason: Retuning is explicit because mean activation changes with tau.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> At fixed rates, longer-lasting spike effects give larger mean activations. The activation difference between two nearby stored values also grows in proportion to $\tau$. In this symmetric comparison, one spike's unit activation change therefore produces a smaller displacement of the stored value: the projection weights scale as $1/\tau$. The spike variance per unit time stays fixed, so the retained variance scales as $1/\tau^2$. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES -->

review.purpose: Explain the inverse-square effect through activation separation and projection.

review.reason: Connects longer spike effects to smaller retained coordinate steps.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> When a recall cue arrives, the stored value has already moved. Later spikes can help estimate the value present at that cue, but they cannot reveal the particular random displacements that occurred before it. Waiting for more spikes also allows the network to move further. paragraphs.text: Separating the error accumulated during storage from the error of reading the cue state makes that question precise. Equal weighting of later observations shows why waiting can become harmful. Allowing for the state's motion then shows how observation can keep helping toward a limit, and how access to only some spikes changes the useful duration. The time constants and noise assumptions also need checking before the resulting limits can be compared with the paper's final error claim.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->

review.purpose: Pose the source-of-drift question and separate data from model.
review.connection: Starts the eye application after memory/readout limits.
review.reason: Recorded shared drive does not by itself identify the proposed circuit.

paragraphs.text: This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory.

review.purpose: Explain why neural diffusion cannot be compared directly with eye motion.
review.connection: Connects memory theory to the downstream motor pathway.
review.reason: Muscle mechanics change the observable trajectory.

paragraphs.text: A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions.

review.purpose: Motivate calibration before the common-noise inference.
review.connection: Previews the pathway, fit and variance analysis that follow.
review.reason: The same physical scale is needed for the later covariance fraction.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

review.purpose: Define storage by the oculomotor integrator.
review.connection: Begins the physical path with the maintained command.
review.reason: An ongoing position signal explains why a memory circuit is relevant.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = NO --> [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings] <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = YES -->

review.purpose: Follow the signal through OMNs, recorded anatomy and ocular plant.
review.connection: Continues from stored position to measured motion.
review.reason: Concrete cell and muscle roles prevent a model variable from being mistaken for the recording.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

review.purpose: Describe the animal task and paired single-cell recording.
review.connection: Grounds the noise inference in what was actually measured.
review.reason: The absence of simultaneous OMN pairs limits direct covariance tests.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments] <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

review.purpose: Describe sampling, exclusions and fixed-length intervals.
review.connection: Specifies the observations used by the subsequent analysis.
review.reason: Repeated intervals and cell count do not create independent animals.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> The position term describes ongoing firing associated with holding the eye at an angle. The velocity term allows a different rate while the eye passes through that same angle. The acceleration term allows another change while its velocity changes. In particular, $m$ is not a direct measurement of the eye's mass. The delay $\Delta t$ is in seconds: firing at time $t$ predicts movement at the later time $t+\Delta t$ for a positive neural lead. paragraphs.text: Here $B$ is the changing position command and $E$ is the eye angle that follows it, both in degrees. The mismatch $B-E$ drives velocity: a command to the right of the current position makes the eye move right. For the same mismatch, a larger response time $\tau$ gives a smaller velocity, so the eye takes longer to catch up and smooths rapid command changes more strongly. This response time belongs to the simplified eye filter. It is not automatically the synaptic decay time used in the memory model.

paragraphs.text: Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width $h$. The Brownian change $\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)$ has mean zero and variance $h$. Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time $t$ is approximately $(\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j$: the initial change has decayed between $u_j$ and $t$.

review.reason: The decayed contribution of each increment makes the calculation followable.

paragraphs.text: The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right. The other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.[^p2-network]

review.purpose: Describe the two integrator populations and their interactions.
review.connection: Introduces the physical model before rate equations.
review.reason: Opposite tuning, excitation and inhibition are concrete reasons the recurrent system can store an angle.

paragraphs.text: For the right population, the model's rate is

review.purpose: Introduce the right-population rate equation.
review.connection: Follows the two-population explanation.
review.reason: The matching left population is then specified through opposite slopes.

paragraphs.text: $E_{OI}$ is the internally represented position in degrees, $\zeta_i^R$ is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and $\lambda_i^0$ is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. $F$ is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, $\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R$. In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by $\zeta_i$.

review.purpose: Define internal angle, tuning slope, offset, rectification and feedback.
review.connection: Interprets the rate equation before synaptic dynamics.
review.reason: The one-degree example states exactly what the slope changes.

paragraphs.text: The model scales each spike train into an input $X_i$ with a saturating mean response. This input changes the neuron's synaptic output $S_i$, the lingering effect of its spikes on neurons receiving them. A weighted difference between the two groups' synaptic outputs gives the represented eye angle $E_{OI}$. This value sets the firing rates again, closing the feedback loop:

review.purpose: Explain spike input, lingering synaptic output and represented-angle feedback.
review.connection: Traces the loop before its equations.
review.reason: The variables act on identifiable cells and outputs.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> Here $\xi_i^R$ is a spike train generated at rate $\lambda_i^R$, $\tau_s$ is the synaptic decay time, and $\lambda_t=60$ Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, $X_i$ and $S_i$ are dimensionless, and the weights $\eta_i$ are in degrees. Between spikes, $S_i$ decays exponentially. One spike adds a jump of $1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]$. Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive $\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)$ that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model's saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.[^p2-network] <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES -->

review.purpose: Explain spike jumps, synaptic decay, units and saturation.
review.connection: Interprets the loop equations.
review.reason: The nonlinear synapse is distinguished from the earlier basic linear model.

Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across $-50$ to $50$ degrees. paragraphs.text: An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The [spike variability section](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-poisson) defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one. The model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. [Such firing is called [**sub-Poisson spiking**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-cv]

review.purpose: Ask how parameter freedom affects an amplitude fit and recall CV.
review.connection: Starts the scaling assessment after the full model.
review.reason: The regular-spike construction is introduced as an assumption to inspect.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> The construction starts with a Poisson process at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of $M$ independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean $1/(M\lambda)$ and variance $1/(M\lambda)^2$. The retained interval therefore has mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/(M\lambda^2)$, and CV $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model. The simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

review.purpose: Construct regular spikes by retaining every Mth Poisson event.
review.connection: Explains the model's CV before using it in count variability.
review.reason: The constant-rate derivation does not automatically apply to varying rates.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. [This is a [**renewal process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed.]{.definition-explanation} Let their mean be $\mu=1/\lambda$ and standard deviation $\sigma_I$. The time to $n$ spikes has variance $n\sigma_I^2$. For a long fixed window $L\simeq n\mu$, a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by $\mu$. Thus <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

review.purpose: Define renewal intervals and derive long-window count variability.
review.connection: Connects interval CV to accumulated fluctuation strength.
review.reason: Independent identically distributed intervals supply the variance addition.

paragraphs.text: This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The [diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) and [information bound](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to $1/\tau_s^2$ and, for a comparable independent population, $1/N$.

paragraphs.text: Could the measured CV itself mostly reflect drift rather than private spike variability? Supplementary Notes test this. Let $\lambda(t)=\bar\lambda+aB(t)$ during a fixation of length $T$, with the rate changes small relative to $\bar\lambda$. For a Brownian path starting at zero, the expected time averaged squared position is $DT$, and the expected squared time mean is $2DT/3$. Subtracting gives the expected within-segment position variance $DT/3=2DT/6$:

review.purpose: Derive the demeaned position variance and inverse-rate expansion.
review.connection: Supplies the two steps used by the drift-CV estimate.
review.reason: The time mean is accounted for rather than treating each position as an independent sample.

These are an order of magnitude check, not a fitted diffusion constant for the whole model. Since one degree is 60 arcmin, that $2D$ equals $0.0278$ deg$^2$/s, or $D=0.0139$ deg$^2$/s.[^p2-cv-drift] <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->
